svg.aria-label: Architecture of the tiny-whoop flight controller firmware. Core 1 runs fc_task at 1000 Hz through six steps: IMU burst read, attitude update, nav snapshot, the control cascade, the motor write and a 1 ms delay. Core 0 runs telemetry_task at 50 Hz and sensor_task at 100 Hz. Three labelled handoffs cross between the cores: an IMU mutex and PID debug queue outward, a spinlocked control frame inward, and a nav-state mutex inward. The IMU and ToF share one I2C bus, the flow sensor is on SPI2 and four motors are driven by LEDC PWM. Off board, a second ESP32-S3 hosts the Wi-Fi dashboard and relays PID tuning traffic to a desktop ground station. A strip along the bottom gives the eight-step startup order.

svg.text: ESP32-S3 Super Mini · ESP-IDF · 240 MHz · FreeRTOS tick 1000 Hz
Three tasks, split by timing sensitivity rather than by subject. The 1 kHz task owns core 1 alone; everything that can block lives on core 0.
one 14-byte I²C burst — accel, temp and gyro
complementary filter, τ = 0.5 s, with the
copy if the sensor task holds it
four LEDC duties, or forced to zero on
phase-locked to the tick; dt is measured,
Nothing in this task may block. Every cross-task read uses a
zero timeout and carries on with its previous copy on failure —
data one tick stale always beats a missed 1 ms deadline.
shared with Wi-Fi, lwIP and IDF background work
always first, whatever else is queued behind it
10 Hz, logging only — not used for control
resync reader: one bad byte costs one frame
every 3rd cycle ≈ 33 Hz, matched to the sensor
altitude · climb rate · body velocity + validity
mutex, 2 ms timeout — skips a publish if busy
A failed read still calls the estimator with NULL — that is what runs the 200 ms validity timeout.
sticks · arm · kill · hold · live gains
50 Hz control frames back to the drone
nothing here can stall the control loop
same I²C0 bus as the IMU
One shared I²C0 bus. imu_setup() creates it inside fc_task, so nothing may touch the ToF until imu_ready_semaphore is given — hence the startup order below.
